summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a suit against Connecticut child protection workers the Second Circuit held that investigators who have a reasonable basis for their substantiation determination do not violate the family's constitutional rights, and affirmed judgment for the defendants.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading Second Circuit case applying the reasonable basis test to a Connecticut child abuse investigation.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that defendants had a reasonable basis for their substantiation determination and that they therefore did not violate plaintiffs' constitutional rights

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Second Circuit held that removing a child on an emergency basis without judicial authorization is unconstitutional when there is reasonable time to obtain a court order safely, and that a state-initiated medical examination of the child implicates Fourth Amendment and bodily integrity interests, although the defendants had qualified immunity because the right was not then clearly established.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that an investigative medical examination of the child implicates the child's Fourth Amendment and bodily integrity interests.
key_cases.quote: it is unconstitutional for state officials to effect a child's removal on an "emergency" basis where there is reasonable time safely to obtain judicial authorization consistent with the child's safety

key_cases.holding: The court held that a mental health professional engaged to evaluate whether children were sexually abused owes no duty of care to the parent suspected of the abuse, because imposing one would deter such evaluations.
key_cases.relevance: It protects the investigative and evaluative stage from tort suits by the person under investigation.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the sounder judicial ruling is to hold that no such duty exists

investigation_requirements: Any visit to or evaluation of a home conducted pursuant to a safety plan must be conducted in person, unless a resident of the home is subject to an order of quarantine or isolation (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 17a-101t, P.A. 24-92, effective July 1, 2024)
